lessons.title: Sentence transformation (made easy)
lessons.summary: Every transformation question (voice, narration, sentence type, tags, linkers, degrees) follows a small fixed pattern, so learn the pattern once and you can change any sentence without changing its meaning.

sections.html:
Active: the doer comes first. Passive: the thing acted on comes first.

  1. Object first: the object (the thing the action is done to) becomes the subject.
  2. be + past participle: put "be" in the same tense as the active verb, then the past participle (third form: typed, written, sent).
  3. by + doer: the doer goes at the end, in object form (by him, by them, by us).
TenseActivePassive
Present simpleThe clerk types the letter.The letter is typed by the clerk.
Present continuousis typingis being typed
Present perfecthas typedhas been typed
Past simpletypedwas typed
Past continuouswas typingwas being typed
Past perfecthad typedhad been typed
Future simplewill typewill be typed
Future perfectwill have typedwill have been typed
Modalscan / must / should typecan / must / should be typed

No passive: present perfect continuous, past perfect continuous, future continuous, future perfect continuous.
✓ The file has been sent by the clerk.
✗ The file has sent by the clerk. (no "been")

Remember for the exam

Find the active tense first; the passive keeps that same tense. Continuous adds "being", perfect adds "been".

Passive of "The peon was cleaning the room":

  1. The room was being cleaned by the peon.
  2. The room was cleaned by the peon.
  3. The room had been cleaned by the peon.

sections.h: Passive of questions, commands and two objects
sections.html:
Questions keep the question form: the helping verb (is, was, did, has) comes before the new subject.
✓ "Did he write the letter?" → Was the letter written by him?
✓ "Who wrote this?" → By whom was this written?
✗ By whom this was written? Commands use Let + object + be + past participle. Polite requests often use "You are requested to…".
✓ "Close the door." → Let the door be closed.
✓ "Please help me." → You are requested to help me.
✗ Let the door closed. Two objects ("gave him a file"): either object can become the subject. The person is the usual choice.
✓ "The manager gave him a file." → He was given a file by the manager. / A file was given to him by the manager. Drop "by" when the doer is unknown or obvious (someone, people, they).
✓ "Someone stole my cycle." → My cycle was stolen. ("My cycle was stolen by someone" is not wrong, but the exam answer drops "by someone".)

Remember for the exam

"Who" becomes "By whom". A command starts with "Let". Unknown doer: drop "by".

Passive of "Post this letter.":

  1. This letter is posted.
  2. Let this letter posted.
  3. Let this letter be posted.

sections.h: Direct to indirect speech: what changes
sections.html:
Indirect (reported) speech drops the quotes and uses "that". Pronouns always change to match the speaker. If the reporting verb (said, told) is past, the tense and the time/place words change too.

WhatDirectIndirect
Pronoun"I", "my"he/she, his/her (match the speaker)
Tense steps backis / am / arewas / were
do / doesdid
did (past)had done
has / will / can / mayhad / would / could / might
Time and placenow, here, this, thesethen, there, that, those
today, tonightthat day, that night
yesterdaythe previous day
tomorrowthe next day
ago, last week, next weekbefore, the previous week, the following week

"Said to me" becomes "told me".
✓ He said, "I am busy today." → He said that he was busy that day.
✗ He said that he is busy today. The tense does NOT change when the words are a universal truth or habit, or when the reporting verb is in the present or future.
✓ The teacher said, "The earth goes round the sun." → The teacher said that the earth goes round the sun.
✓ He says, "I am tired." → He says that he is tired.

Remember for the exam

Reporting verb in the past: shift tense one step back and change the time words. Truth or "says": no shift.

Indirect form of: She said, "I will come tomorrow."

  1. She said that I would come the next day.
  2. She said that she will come tomorrow.
  3. She said that she would come the next day.

Yes/no questions: asked + if/whether, then normal statement order, and a full stop, not a question mark.
✓ He said to me, "Have you finished the report?" → He asked me if I had finished the report.
✗ He asked me had I finished the report? Wh-questions (where, what, why…): asked + the wh-word, then subject + verb.
✓ She said to me, "Where do you live?" → She asked me where I lived.
✗ She asked me where did I live. Commands and requests: told / ordered / requested + person + to + verb. For "don't", use not to.
✓ The officer said to the peon, "Bring the file." → The officer ordered the peon to bring the file.
✓ He said to me, "Please wait." → He requested me to wait.
✓ She said to him, "Don't shout." → She told him not to shout. Exclamations: exclaimed (with joy, sorrow, surprise) that + statement.
✓ He said, "What a fine day it is!" → He exclaimed that it was a very fine day.
✓ She said, "Alas! I have lost my purse." → She exclaimed with sorrow that she had lost her purse.

Remember for the exam

Indirect questions never keep "do/did" before the subject and never end with "?".

Indirect form of: He said to me, "Why are you late?"

  1. He told me why I was late.
  2. He asked me why was I late.
  3. He asked me why I was late.

• Simple: one main clause, one finite verb (a verb with a tense). "Being ill, he did not come."
  • Compound: two main clauses joined by and, but, or, so. "He was ill, so he did not come."
  • Complex: one main clause plus a dependent clause starting with because, as, since, although, when, if, who, that. "As he was ill, he did not come."
CompoundComplexSimple
He was ill, so he did not come.As he was ill, he did not come.Being ill, he did not come.
He is poor, but he is honest.Although he is poor, he is honest.In spite of being poor, he is honest.
He is very weak, so he cannot walk.He is so weak that he cannot walk.He is too weak to walk.

✓ Although he is poor, he is honest.
✗ Although he is poor, but he is honest. (two linkers for one join)
✗ As he was ill, so he did not come.

Remember for the exam

One linker per join. "Although/as" makes it complex; "but/so" makes it compound; a phrase (being, in spite of, too…to) makes it simple.

Simple form of "As he was tired, he went to bed early."

  1. As he was tired, so he went to bed early.
  2. He was tired, so he went to bed early.
  3. Being tired, he went to bed early.

Statement ↔ question (rhetorical question with the same meaning): a positive statement becomes a negative question, and the reverse.
✓ "Everyone loves his country." → Who does not love his country?
✓ "Nobody can bribe him." → Who can bribe him?
✓ "It is no use crying." → What is the use of crying? Affirmative ↔ negative without changing the meaning: use the opposite word, or "none but".
✓ "Only a fool would say this." → None but a fool would say this.
✓ "Everyone was present." → No one was absent.
✗ None but a fool would not say this. Question tags: positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. Use the same helping verb and a pronoun.

StatementTag
He is late,isn't he?
She didn't come,did she?
I am right,aren't I?
Let's start,shall we?
Close the door,will you?
He hardly works,does he?
Nobody came,did they?
There is a bus,isn't there?

Hardly, seldom, never, scarcely and nobody count as negative, so their tag is positive.

Remember for the exam

"I am" → aren't I. "Let's" → shall we. A "hardly / never / nobody" sentence takes a positive tag.

Choose the tag: "She never tells lies, ___?"

  1. does she
  2. doesn't she
  3. isn't she

sections.h: Conjunctions and linkers the exam tests
sections.html:
Some linkers come in fixed pairs. Swap one half and the sentence is wrong.

LinkerCorrect shapeWrong
no soonerNo sooner had he left than it rained.…when it rained
hardly / scarcelyHardly had I sat down when the phone rang.…than the phone rang
not onlyHe is not only honest but also hard-working.…and also hard-working
either / neithereither tea or coffee; neither tea nor coffeeneither…or
as soon asAs soon as he left, it rained. (= No sooner had he left than it rained.)
lestWalk carefully lest you should fall.lest you should not fall
unlessUnless you hurry, you will miss the bus.Unless you do not hurry
thoughThough he is rich, yet he is humble. (or no "yet")Though…but
so…thatHe spoke so fast that nobody understood.
too…toThe box is too heavy to lift.too heavy that

✓ No sooner had the bell rung than the clerks left.
✗ No sooner the bell rang than the clerks left. (needs "had + subject + past participle") "Lest" already means "so that … not", and "unless" already means "if not", so never add another "not".

Remember for the exam

No sooner → than. Hardly/scarcely → when. Lest → should. Unless → no "not".

"___ you work hard, you will not pass."

  1. Unless
  2. Lest
  3. Neither

Adjectives have three degrees: positive (big), comparative (bigger), superlative (biggest). One fact can be written in all three.

Degree"The best" form"One of the best" form
SuperlativeKolkata is the biggest city in West Bengal.Delhi is one of the biggest cities in India.
ComparativeKolkata is bigger than any other city in West Bengal.Delhi is bigger than most other cities in India.
PositiveNo other city in West Bengal is as big as Kolkata.Very few cities in India are as big as Delhi.

For two people: "Ram is taller than Shyam" → "Shyam is not as tall as Ram."
✓ Kolkata is bigger than any other city in West Bengal.
✗ Kolkata is bigger than any city in West Bengal. (Kolkata is itself a city in West Bengal; you need "other")
✗ Kolkata is the most biggest city. (double superlative)

Remember for the exam

"The …est" ↔ "…er than any other" ↔ "No other … as … as". "One of the …est" ↔ "…er than most other" ↔ "Very few … as … as".

Positive form of "This is the cleanest office in the building."

  1. This office is cleaner than any office in the building.
  2. No other office in the building is as clean as this.
  3. No office is cleaner than any other office.

• Voice: same tense, be + past participle; "Who" → "By whom"; commands → "Let … be …".
  • Four continuous tenses (present perfect, past perfect, future and future perfect continuous) have no passive.
  • Narration: past reporting verb → tense back one step, time words change (tomorrow → the next day). Universal truth or "says": no change.
  • Indirect questions: if/whether or wh-word, statement order, full stop.
  • Commands: told/ordered/requested + to; "don't" → not to.
  • One linker per join: never "although … but" or "as … so".
  • No sooner … than; hardly/scarcely … when; lest … should; unless with no "not".
  • Tags: "I am" → aren't I; "Let's" → shall we; hardly/never → positive tag.
"By" is not always the preposition

Some passives take another preposition. "Everyone knows him" → He is known to everyone. "Water filled the tank" → The tank was filled with water. If "by" sounds odd after known or filled, the exam wants "to" or "with".

facts: Active → passive in 3 steps
Object becomes subject; verb becomes be + past participle (in the same tense as the active verb); doer goes after "by"
Continuous and perfect passives
Continuous adds "being" (is being typed); perfect adds "been" (has / had / will have been typed)
Tenses with no passive
Present perfect continuous, past perfect continuous, future continuous, future perfect continuous
Passive of a command
Let + object + be + past participle (Let the door be closed); a request: "You are requested to…"
Reporting verb in the past: tense steps back
is → was, has → had, will → would, can → could, does → did, did → had done
When the tense does NOT change in indirect speech
Universal truth or habit, or a reporting verb in the present or future (says, will say)
Indirect question
asked + if/whether or the wh-word + statement word order, ending with a full stop
Indirect command
told / ordered / requested + person + to + verb; "don't" becomes "not to"
No sooner / hardly / scarcely
No sooner had + subject + past participle … than; Hardly/Scarcely had … when
Superlative → comparative → positive
the biggest → bigger than any other → No other … is as big as
too … to
= so … that … not (too weak to walk = so weak that he cannot walk)
traps: "Although … but" and "As … so" are wrong: one linker per join. "Though … yet" is the one such pair that is allowed.
"No sooner … when" and "Hardly … than" are wrong: no sooner goes with than, hardly/scarcely with when.
Indirect questions take statement order and no question mark: "asked where I lived", not "asked where did I live?".
"Lest … should not" and "Unless … not" are wrong: lest and unless already contain the "not".
recap: Passive: object first, be + past participle in the same tense, by + doer (drop "by" if the doer is unknown).
Questions: "Who" → "By whom"; commands: "Let … be + past participle".
Indirect speech: past reporting verb shifts the tense back and changes now/here/today/tomorrow; truths and "says" do not shift.
Simple (one finite verb, a phrase), compound (and/but/so), complex (because/although/when/if): change the linker, keep the meaning.
Tags flip positive/negative; "I am" → aren't I, "Let's" → shall we; degrees: the …est = …er than any other = no other … as … as.

mcqs.q: Change into passive: "The peon is cleaning the room."
o: The room is being cleaned by the peon.
The room is cleaned by the peon.
The room has been cleaned by the peon.
The room was being cleaned by the peon.
mcqs.e: "Is cleaning" is present continuous, so the passive is "is being cleaned".

mcqs.q: Change into passive: "The clerk had sent the file."
o: The file was sent by the clerk.
The file had been sent by the clerk.
The file had sent by the clerk.
The file has been sent by the clerk.
mcqs.e: Past perfect "had sent" becomes "had been sent". "Had sent" without "been" is still active.

mcqs.q: Change into passive: "Who broke the window?"
o: Whom was the window broken?
By whom the window was broken?
By whom was the window broken?
By whom was the window being broken?
mcqs.e: "Who" becomes "By whom", and the question keeps "was" before the subject. Past simple "broke" gives "was broken", not "was being broken".

o: The gate was opened.
Let the gate opened.
Let the gate is opened.
Let the gate be opened.
mcqs.e: A command becomes Let + object + be + past participle.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I am busy today."
o: He said that he was busy today.
He said that he is busy today.
He said that I was busy that day.
He said that he was busy that day.
mcqs.e: I → he, am → was, today → that day. Every other option misses one of these changes.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "Where do you work?"
o: She asked me where did I work.
She asked me where I worked.
She asked me where do you work.
She told me where I worked.
mcqs.e: A question takes "asked", the wh-word, then statement order (I worked) with "do" removed and the tense shifted back.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: The officer said to the peon, "Do not open the window."
o: The officer ordered the peon not to open the window.
The officer ordered the peon not open the window.
The officer told the peon that do not open the window.
The officer asked the peon if not to open the window.
mcqs.e: A negative command becomes ordered/told + person + not to + verb.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Have you finished the report?"
o: He asked me if I had finished the report.
He asked me if I have finished the report?
He told me if I had finished the report.
He asked me that whether I had finished the report.
mcqs.e: Yes/no question: asked + if, statement order, have → had, full stop. Never "that whether".

mcqs.q: Change into a complex sentence: "He was ill, so he could not attend office."
o: He being ill, so he could not attend office.
Being ill, he could not attend office.
As he was ill, so he could not attend office.
As he was ill, he could not attend office.
mcqs.e: "As he was ill" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex. "Being ill" makes a simple sentence, and "as … so" uses two linkers.

mcqs.q: Change into a complex sentence: "In spite of his poverty, he is honest."
o: Although he is poor, he is honest.
Although he is poor, but he is honest.
He is poor, but he is honest.
In spite of he is poor, he is honest.
mcqs.e: "Although" starts a dependent clause: complex. "He is poor, but…" is compound, and "although … but" is a double linker.

mcqs.q: Rewrite without "too": "He is too weak to walk."
o: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
He is so weak that he can walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.
He is very weak to walk.
mcqs.e: too … to = so … that … not. "Too … that" is never correct.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct question tag: "I am late, ___?"
o: don't I
isn't it
am not I
aren't I
mcqs.e: The standard tag for "I am" is "aren't I".

mcqs.q: Choose the correct question tag: "He hardly ever comes on time, ___?"
o: didn't he
doesn't he
is he
does he
mcqs.e: "Hardly" makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive; "comes" is present simple, so "does he".

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank: "No sooner had the train left ___ it started raining."
o: when
than
then
as
mcqs.e: "No sooner" always pairs with "than". "When" goes with hardly/scarcely.

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank: "Walk carefully lest you ___ fall."
o: would not
should not
will not
should
mcqs.e: "Lest" means "so that … not" and is followed by "should". Adding "not" doubles the negative.

Merriam-Webster: comprise (usage note on comprised of)
